meta.q: What does the H-Net paper say about byte-level modeling?

text: The H‑Net paper emphasizes that its architecture is designed specifically for **byte‑level modeling**.  It shows that H‑Net can operate directly on raw byte streams without any handcrafted vocabulary or token‑boundary cues, and that this byte‑level approach yields better compression and lower bits‑per‑byte than both BPE‑based Transformers and a space‑only byte model (see Figure 5) [2507.07955v2 §3.2 pp.15‑16].  The authors also compare H‑Net to other byte‑level baselines, noting that H‑Net is the first architecture to provide **dynamic, multi‑stage hierarchies** for byte‑level data and that it outperforms a sparsified byte‑level isotropic Transformer (LlamaByte) even when matched for parameters and FLOPs [2507.07955v2 §3.3 pp.20‑21].  Moreover, they argue that H‑Net’s form of dynamic sparsity (conditional computation) is more semantically meaningful than generic Mixture‑of‑Experts sparsity for byte‑level tasks [2507.07955v2 §4 p.23].  Finally, experiments demonstrate that pure Transformer configurations perform poorly on byte sequences, while incorporating Mamba (state‑space) layers—especially in a hierarchical byte‑level pipeline—significantly improves compression efficiency and modeling performance [2507.07955v2 §3.3 p.19].

meta.q: How is residual dropout used in the Transformer paper?

text: In the Transformer model, dropout is applied to the **residual connections**. Specifically, the paper states that dropout is “applied to the output of each sub‑layer, before it is added to the sub‑layer input and normalized” [1706.03762v7 §5.4 pp.7‑8]. In addition, dropout is also applied to the summed token embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks. For the base model the dropout probability is set to P₍drop₎ = 0.1.

meta.q: How is full-duplex dialogue used in the Moshi paper?

text: Moshi achieves full‑duplex spoken dialogue by **modeling two parallel streams of tokens – one for the user’s speech and one for Moshi’s own speech – each composed of hierarchical semantic and acoustic tokens**.  This multi‑stream architecture lets the system **listen and speak at the same time**, removing the need for explicit speaker‑turn boundaries and handling overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections.  Because the model generates both streams jointly (with the text‑language‑model backbone Helium providing linguistic knowledge), it can exploit all linguistic and non‑linguistic information from the user while producing its response in real time【2410.00037v1 §2 pp.5‑6】.  The paper therefore describes Moshi as “the first real‑time, full‑duplex spoken dialogue system” that “allows for full‑duplex spoken dialogue with a user thanks to an innovative architecture”【2410.00037v1 §3.1 pp.6‑7】.
